title: Rise and shine! A century of Macy’s balloons.
text:
Rise and shine! A century of Macy’s balloons.
On the 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade, one man is credited with stringing it all together.
Did you know that when you watch the enormous balloons float through New York City during the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, you’re also watching the world’s largest puppet show – and a hundred years of American history?
This year marks the 100th Macy’s parade. Around 3.5 million people cram the streets every year to catch a glimpse of the balloons in person. And last year, as families around the country gathered to celebrate Thanksgiving, a record 34 million people watched the event live on TV. That’s almost 10% of the entire U.S. population!
A number of new balloons join the lineup this year, including two iconic versions of parade favorites: “Joe Cool” Snoopy and “Sorcerer’s Apprentice” Mickey Mouse. But alongside these larger-than-life inflatable characters, a new float represents a real person: Tony Sarg.
On Thanksgiving morning, millions tune in to the iconic Macy’s parade. The “father of the Macy’s balloons” shares the history behind the gigantic inflatables that are brought to life each year.
To understand why people call Mr. Sarg the “father of the Macy’s balloons,” let’s take a step back to the very first Macy’s parade on Nov. 27, 1924. The parade has run every year since, except for a three-year period during the Second World War.
“Macy’s employees created the first parade,” explains Emily Pazar, assistant curator of decorative arts and material culture at The New York Historical, in a statement via email. Many of them were immigrants, inspired by festival and parade traditions from their home countries. (A Macy’s representative did not answer a request for comment by publication time.)
The first parade followed a six-mile route from Harlem to Herald Square. Along with hundreds of employees dressed as clowns and nursery rhyme characters, the parade featured live animals from Central Park Zoo.
Originally known as the Macy’s Christmas Parade, it was meant to officially kick off the holiday shopping season. As part of the first parade’s grand finale, a man dressed as Santa Claus climbed on top of the Macy’s entrance and unveiled the beloved Macy’s holiday window displays.
But since snarling lions and smelly elephants didn’t exactly put kids in the Christmas mood, Macy’s turned to Tony Sarg to come up with something new. Mr. Sarg, a successful commercial artist and puppeteer, was designing Macy’s window displays at the time. He looked around his studio in New York City, and thought about how much children loved the dancing characters in his touring puppet show, “Tony Sarg’s Marionettes.” He had an idea: What if the world’s largest parade could become the world’s largest puppet show?
“He filled a balloon with air, and held it up by a team of handlers on poles,” says Stephanie Plunkett, chief curator of the Norman Rockwell Museum and co-curator of the “Tony Sarg: Genius at Play” exhibit.
The massive inflatable puppets were an instant hit. But because they weren’t visible to everyone in the crowd, Mr. Sarg got creative. The following year, he filled the balloons with helium, held down with strings by teams of puppeteers.
Floating almost as high as the buildings themselves, Mr. Sarg’s invention has dazzled New Yorkers almost every Thanksgiving Day since.
One reason the parade continues to enchant Americans, Ms. Pazar writes, is how it evolves with popular culture. New balloons and floats feature popular characters (Hint: Look for Bluey and Bob the Minion this year!) while “always being rooted in the spirit of past editions.”
So, if you spot the “Tony Sarg’s Amazing Marionettes” float in this year’s parade, remember the creativity and ambition of the puppeteer who made it all happen. Mr. Sarg’s legacy shows any aspiring artist, Ms. Plunkett says, why “you have to create the things you love, and find a place for them.”
